blocks.x: I was going to ask if you could give your name.
John C. Pope.
And this is in Mobile, of course. What is your address here? 502 South Dearborn Street. And I wanted to ask when you were born, just the date.

1883, November 23rd. So you're 76 years old. 76 years old, this year. Now, as I'm saying, the Excelsior Band was practically born, you understand, on the day that I was born. And I was getting together. My father and his friends. And they organized a band and named it the Excelsior Band, you see.
Why did they choose Excelsior as a name? I don't know. But it was in honor of your birth. That's right.
Your father was Alexander Pope. That's right. John Alexander Pope.
But do you know when he was born? About how old he was when you were born?
Well, no, I don't know if he got to the date. But I know he would have been just a matter of which. That when he died, he would have been 88 years old. And when did he die?
About?
Oh, he died about seven years ago, seven or eight years ago.
We didn't miss him by long.
No. And I'm saying now, back in his days, they practically done almost the same way that we've done during my career. Which I'd taken over, oh, I should say around about 19-8.
Uh-huh.
Nineteen seven or 19-8. Uh-huh.
And I carried on for about 28 years. And did you say that you played the cornet? I played the trumpet. The trumpet. And your father played the cornet or trumpet? The cornet.
He played E-flat. E-flat. And I started going to the cornet that you have there. Yes. Short the cornet like that. Yes. Yes.
Yes. Was the latter days why. Did you have three cornet players in the band, three trumpet players?
We had around four at all times. Four. Four. How many were in the excel of your band? Fourteen.
Fourteen. And there was four trumpet, three alto players, you know the old time altos. Yes. And two trombone, baritone, bass, two drummers.
Once in a while we'd pick up a paramedic player, another summer. But not all the time? No, not all the time.
Did they have any saxophones in those days? No. Well, yes they did. But we didn't use them. In the latter days we did. When did you start to use the saxophone?
Do you use the saxophone? No, what year did they start to use the saxophone in the band?

Well, I'll say around... The twenties or thirties? Oh, around... I'll say around the twenties? Uh-huh. 1920s. Yeah, 1920s. Yes. And I'm saying we played funeral parades. You did play funeral parades? We played funeral parades on an average two or three times a week.
Oh, you did?
Yes.
Now when did they start playing? Very long. How recently have they played funerals?
Oh, I guess that's been now over twenty years.
No funerals for the last twenty years?
You don't use them anymore. No, don't use them at all. All the organizations, you know, and... Yes. Each one had one, but a member would die, they would play some music.
They still do that over at New Orleans.

They would play such music as going out to the cemetery, funeral marches, going to the cemetery, and coming back, you had... You played regular popular music. Yes. In other words, I remember what we played very often. So glad to go and rescue you.
Yes.

Bye-bye, you black boy, and all those kind of things, you know. Yes, yes. Yes. Great days. Then we made parades for the different organizations. We're parading the afternoons from three until six o'clock.
Were those on Sundays or any day in a week? Any day in a week. Almost any day. Monday was the famous... Monday and Wednesday was the regular days.
Right. And on that night, we'd return around eight o'clock to the place where they would have the dance. Yes. Then we'd put into music to the dance with the same band.
Same band, same instruments.
Same band, yes. Same band, same band.
Same band.
Same band. You had fourteen men in the dance band? Fourteen men in the dance band.
That's right.
We had... We played all the popular airs, you know, just as they come up.
Yes.

And the same... That was colored. We made those plays, you know. Yes. Now we played all the white dances downtown, which we had the famous band in town. We played the Battle House, Country Club, and the Athelston Club, all that was big...
Did you always play written music or did you play written music? Or did you sometimes play... No, no, no, no.
Sometimes we'd pick up or something, you know. They were very good at that. Yes.
Yes.
Coming back from the cemetery, I guess you played by head or by ear? I don't mean by ear or by music. Yes. We had music, sure.
We always used music.
Yes.
We were rehearsing on an average twice a week. And if a member of the band wasn't there at that time, why, he was fine. So, you know, back in those days, 25 cents, for instance.
Yes. Yes. You mentioned the Trenier brothers, I think it was. Trenier, yes.

Trenier. Now, he's the father of the Trenier brothers. They're very famous right now. Because they just left Vegas, I think, back home. They moved from Mobile to Los Angeles. And he's one that still lives. I have another one that lives now. It's called Willie Bolero. What was that name?
Willie Bolero.

Bolero, like a Spanish name. Bolero, yes. And, of course, he was one of the late members, you know. He just trained him myself. He'd come along and go every day, you know. But my father practically gives it up.

There was one musician I was going to ask about. I met a male man downtown this morning who is a musician too. And he told me there was a fellow, he didn't know his real name, they just call him Chicken. And he's a jazz at the cathedral.
Well, that's Bolero. That's Bolero. Oh, that's... That's Bolero. That's right. And he's still in town.
He's still in town, yes. And he used to play with the Excelsior band.

He used to play with the Excelsior band, the original band. What did he play? He played alto. Alto? Alto, hi. He's the man. You know, he played, you know, ta, Yes, I know that. You know what I'm talking about.

Yes, indeed. This male man I met, his name is Thomas Daley. Thomas Daley? Thomas Daley Senior. And he knows this man. He knows you, too. You mentioned this other man was about your age, he thought, or maybe even older.

That's right. He may be a year older than I have. That's Bolero, we have reference. Yes. So we'll get to see. Well, Daley, back in the middle, I think you might have met some of the younger... Probably.
He was a younger man. He was a male man.
I don't think he played with the Excelsior band.
No. No. He plays sax, clarinet, and trumpet. Yes, sir. Three instruments. When you started in music, did you start right on the cornet first?
No, I had what you call a vowel trombone. Oh, you did. That was very short, just probably a month or so, you know, I changed to the trumpet.
Did your father give you lessons?
No, not my father. By the name of Mr. Norman Cox, he's dead now. And the punk brunette, they were teachers back in those days. Yes. And I felt one of those fellows.
In fact, most all of us did.
Mm-hmm.
What was the music like when you, the first music you remember hearing the band play? Did they play those popular pieces in charge of jazzy and time? That's right. Kind of jazzy time.

Ragtime. Ragtime back in those days, you know. Even when you were a boy. We played all the famous marches, quite a bit of Susan's marches. Yes. All heavy marches, you know. The kick that we got out of playing those kind of things, when they bring those bands from St. Louis, Chicago, down in the for Carnival, you know, we used to Carnival marches out of the government street. Yes. And we'd meet the little 14th piece band and put them out of commission, you know. Used to blast away, you know. They'd have probably 40, 50 million in the band.
Why did they stop doing funerals? Do you know why they stopped doing funerals?
No, I don't know just exactly. I think it was financial conditions. Financial? Yes, I think so.
But the lodges and the organizations still exist in Mobile, were they? No.

The insurance put those people out of business, most of them, you know. They couldn't comply with the laws, you know, the state laws and so on. So finally they'd given up. Now we used to, those organizations, I'm saying, they had quite a few in Mobile. And they used to give picnics, you understand, once or twice a year and accumulate a few hundred dollars, you know. And we used to pay those picnics for them. And after that was cut out, after the band broken up to understand, I gave myself, blamed myself in a way, you know, I gave it all up. And after that, no one was very much interested in the band, you see. And so, I gradually put the organizations out of business. Because they didn't get that stuff, that extra money.
I'm wondering, did the bands ever play on any boats? Did they have boats that out on the ground?
Yes, we played all on those bay boats, you know, across, going across on the other side of the Baltimore County. We played dances on those boats quite often. For dancing.
Did it have regular excursion boats like on the Mississippi River? Yes. That's right.

That's right. We had a good many of them, yeah. From time to time, you know. We had the Pleasure Bay and the Corny and the Mary Queen and boats of that kind, you know. We used to meet down at the foot of Dauphin Street and taking a large crowd. That was almost quite a white.
Did you have any competition with other bands or just?

Well, yes, we did. Back in those days, we had Mr. Drago, Cummins, and they were all white bands, you know. White band. Yes. Then we had a few colored bands, but they never did wake up to that point since then.
I imagine you had visits in Mobile from some of the other bands from New Orleans.
Well, yes, we did. That is, orchestras, you know.
Do you remember some of the men that came over here that you heard?
Well, I remember Sam Morgan and this man that died some time ago. I think he prayed for the president.
Oh, Celestine. Celestine.
Celestine. All the people like that, you know. Did you ever remember?
Robichaux. Robichaux.
Yeah, people like that, they came over here.

Remember Buddy Petit? Did he play over here? Who's that Buddy Petit? No, I don't remember. Or Chris Pelley? No, I don't remember that. There's another man, an old time trumpet that told me once about your father, Bunk Johnson. Did you ever meet him? No, I don't think that either. Bunk Johnson. No, I don't think that either. They tell me once that your father, I've been told that they would play on Mardi Gras day, the boat would come in with some of the organizations. Did they do that?
Do you remember? Yes, I did. King, queen, they would come in.

I played all those. People told me that your father used to be famous that the word they used, they played a lot of flourishes, like bugle calls or something that the king would come in. That's right. What kind of bugle calls were they? What was white?

I don't recall just the right tiles for them, you know. But it's something you made up? They would come in, you know. They would call the bugle calls, and bury me, you know. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Like that. That's it. I just wish I had a little time, you understand? Well, that's all right.
That's fine. You're telling us everything we want to know about it. It's wonderful to hear it. You know?

Yes. So, as I'm saying now, at the present time, Mr. Eddie Langston, he has the band. I said, he'll get together, you know. Yeah. Yeah, for the carnival. But after I'd given it up, there was a Charlie Lifstein that played with me. He'd taken the band over. Well, it's short-lived, you know. Didn't have it very long. And after he died, this Langston's taking it over.

So there were breaks in the band's history when the band was not playing? How's that? Yes. And then somebody else reformed the band? Is that right? Yes, that's right. Yes, sir. What do you think of the way they play now? Well, I like it very much. What sort of...
Do they change different type of music now to the old stuff? Well, no.
They play the regular same music, you know. They do. How many are in the band today? Oh, I think they must have about the same amount, around 14.
14. Yeah, about 14. But with saxophones now, and taradets too. Yeah, they use taradets, saxophones. Do they use E-flat taradets or ordinary B-flats? No, all B-flats.
B-flats.
Do they have more than one? They have more than one? They might have one too.
Do they play from music most of the time or just head arrangements?
No, they have arrangements. Yes, yes. I want to play a tradition.
But no more funeral marches, just quick time now.
Yes, sir.
Parade music.
Yes, sir. I wondered, the dance bands you heard, like Sam Morgan and the other ones that came over from New Orleans, did they have a different style of music than the local people played?
Yes, they did. They had that original jazz, you know, ragtime we called it back in those days.
Did they play more ragtime, you think, the New Orleans bands, than you did here?

Oh, yes, sir. I was on the show and practically put me out of business. The business bands did. They'd come over here in the late years, you know, and play that jazz music, you know, which we call ragtime, we played strictly by the music.
Did you ever go to New Orleans yourself when you were younger?
No, I never did.
But you used to hear them when they came here?
Yes, they come here, that's right.
I wondered, did your father ever, I don't like to keep bothering you about your father because naturally you don't know everything.
Well, back in his days, they made trips in Yard River to South of Bay. They did? Yes, they made trips on them. They went on excursions, yes, and played dancing over there.
Would that be on the train or the folk? On the train, on the train.
On the train, on the train.
Training excursions. Yes, that's right. Did your father ever talk about where he learned music, if he picked it up himself, or if he had a teacher, or what he did?
I don't remember. I don't remember.
What sort of uniforms did the band wear?

We had just about a good uniform as the other band in the country had. They were made by Pettibon, I remember the name very well. Back in those days, they paid as much as 35 to 40 dollars each uniform, which I would have.
you know, back in those days. Of course, just somewhere around, everybody ended up with a hundred dollars.
What did it look like? What color was it?

Well, I do remember one time they had a dark uniform trimmed in light gold triplet. Very pretty, very small. A black uniform was it? Something kind. Black and gold? Yes, blue, something in that time. And back in my day, we had the regulation uniform. Yes. Did they have a pink cap? The Federalist of Musician uniform. Back in my father's days, while they had, as I'm saying, they had the choice, you understand? As I come along, while we had the Federalist of Musician stop. Yes.
Oh, you have some pictures of the... This is my grandfather.
Oh, that's right, yes? Oh, yeah. Yeah, he is. Yes. My grandfather.
Oh, yes. It's quite a resemblance, actually.
I mean, the way your father looks there. Well, I was about 35 years old when I had that picture made.
You look a good day like your father. Very much. Very much like that. Yes. Thank you very much for getting to see you.

Thank you. You have a picture of me all. You know, they... I had four daughters. They sang in New York, you know. Stayed there quite a while. Until one died, I broke up the key. Really? Yes. They gave them pretty well. Mm-hmm. They stayed there quite a while. They went to Canada and stayed there two, three months. In one place. Mm-hmm.
Do you have any photographs of the band? How is that? Do you have any photographs of the Excelsior band? No.
I don't know. This is when we went for the show business.
Oh, yes. Very, very, very good. Four sisters.

Four sisters. Yes. All of them are the daughters. Great, man. I was going to ask about the marches. Do you remember how you would line up who was in front and who was in back in the arms? Yes, I do remember that.
Well, we all lined up the larger instruments. For instance, the bass, baritone, two trombones. The rest of four, you know, and then the alto players and the trumpets and the drums in the back.
The drums are always in back then. Right. They do that in New Orleans. Yes. I suppose it's a standard over there. And always four abreast then. That's right.
That's right. Just 14 men.
Did they march as fast then? The Army and high school bands all march so fast that they almost run.

We had a different step, you understand, than what the U is now. We had a longer stride than what... You have to swing. Yes. That's right. Longer stride. Now they use a little short. I don't know what you might call that... That's right.
Yes, yes.
Yeah, they used to go swinging down the street, but they do not do hard. Did they usually play a little bit slower, the marches, than they do today, you think? No, I think they're about the same.

Just about the same. They're all different. It was the steps, you understand, that they make now. They make short steps. We had a longer stride with us. Do you remember any of the other marches? You mentioned Sousa marches. Did they ever play High Society? High Society?
That was my favorite. Panama. Panama. Panama. Panama.
I think that was one we played. We played that. So many other heavy marches, you know.
Yes.

Very good. Pretty good on that. You take your head, clarinet pots, cue it in. We take that up with the trumpet. With the trumpet? With the trumpet. With the trumpet. We did all of that. Last night you began to tell us a little bit about the dance arrangement when you play for dances. You used the same, you used the same, you used the same, you used the same, you used the instrument, you used the same, you used the same, you used the same, you used the
stuff you used the same brass band lineup? That same brass band lineup. 14 pieces inside of

14, that's right. Of course in the latter days I organized my own orchestra and we had another orchestra by the name of Holman's. Holman. Orchestra, yes. And I played with him 18 years and after that I organized my own as known as Hoops Dreamland Serenators. How many were in that about? Well we had an average around eight to nine. Eight to nine. Did you use the bass or piano or guitar or anything in those? Well yeah we had the guitar, we had the bass, the piano, trumpet, three saxophones and drums. And for years I attended principal work in Mobile. All the big society dances out of town I played all those dances. That's what used to band all the time. Did you play mostly for music or did you have ear or head arrangements? Mostly by music. Mostly by music. Sometimes we'd pick up something very popular by air and we'd done pretty well with that. Did you add a little bit to it? That is sort of as they say, douse it up or make it raggy? Well we did. We did do that. We made it a little raggy as you say.
I wondered when the full band played they used two drummers inside. That's right, two drummers. One fellow hitting the bass drum. You used the bass drum for dancing too?
Well we had track drums then. We called them back to the band. I don't know what you call them now.
Now on your parade did the bass drummer play a cymbal to one hand?
That's right. They have cymbal, lift head and... Use a wire meter. That's right.
Like they... We used all those kinds of things.
Yes.

In the old days for the dance bands, when you first had a small group for the dance bands, did they always use piano or did sometime you play without a piano? Well we very suddenly played without a piano. Because in New Orleans a lot of the bands just used... they didn't have a... Yes sir. A lot of the little taverns and basses they still don't have a piano so they'll play without just using guitar and bass. I wondered if they did that much here.

Well we played with the piano most of the time. Always had a piano playing. In fact, I had one of the best piano players I believe... well... I don't know what he... he composed some music and he was an arranger for some concern in Chicago.

American Conservancy. Who's that? American Conservancy. Oh the American... I was in Chicago. I knew that. Edward Wright. Edward Wright. Yeah, he was Edward Wright. He's still there. He's in a cast now. Edward Wright. Uh-huh. Edward Wright. He's very interested to talk to him. He's in a cast. He was run old for years... about a couple of years ago.
Oh, I understand. Edward Wright. Yeah. I was going to ask... did you know Cootie Williams? Yes, Cootie played with me quite a bit.

Did he play with you too? Yes, Cootie played with me quite a bit. Back he started right out playing with me right here in Mobile. Somebody once... I went to New York one time and he and Duke Ellington, they wanted me to play in his band. Oh really? As I told him about that time, I was less too old now. I couldn't compete with those fellows in the bank of that band. Those bands. Yes, Cootie played with me quite a while.
Somebody told me that Cootie's teacher was Charles Lipscomb. How do you pronounce that name? Is that the man you were telling about? Lipscomb? Lipscomb. That's right.

Give all the information. Make it honest now while you're in. I'm calling. I don't. Good. Looked like you brought your band. So I says, the seltzer band. So I put it in the announcement. I says, the seltzer band's going to play. So then I asked one of the men, I says, now what's this seltzer band? They said, the men always say, well, that's the excelsior band. The seltzer band. So that's another phase of your evening.

Well, I tell you, we were the drawing card back in those days, you know. Every time we mentioned the seltzer band, I meant the public was coming out. That's pretty well. I'm saying the seltzer band now is, would be seven, six years old.
Did the band have a large following, a second line, as they say?

Yes, yes, yes. And sometimes they had to have an officer, you understand, to take the crowd away. Really? But if you have Mardi Gras, you would have probably five or six bands, you know, and the seltzer band had the crowd. And the masters, you know, on the foot, they would be hung for the seltzer band. I can hear them now calling for folk. You know what I mean? The seltzer band with them. Yes.
And now they only play on a conical day, do they? Just once a year. Once a year. And who is the leader now?

Langston. Edward Langston. Edward Langston. Yeah, I wish I could have gotten known to him by that time I'd have him here with me. He's a trumpet player, is he? No, he's a saxophone player. Saxophone. And saxophone. We'll see in our next trip, then we'll find him. Yes. I'll try to get him something, you know, kind of intelligently. As I'm saying right now, I don't know just what I'm talking about. This is very good.
You see, there's a good history of it. But I imagine they play a different style to the way the old band used to play.

Well, I don't think so. You don't think they have? Because we played all the popular... Of course, you know, as a whole, music has changed a little bit, you know. Yes. I think back to my days, music was more simplified than what it is right now.
Yes. What sort of age would you say the men in the band are today? The average age of the men in the band today?

What is playing today? Yes. Oh, they're around... In the 20s, I should think. Oh, they're young. They're young. 30 years old. Are there any old time now? Well, all those time has practically died out in the last few years. That did play along with those youngsters. Yes.
Yes.
Next year, about the oldest one now. That's 11.
How old is he?
Oh, next door would be somewhere else... We have the 60s. Any 60s? No, I won't say he's that old. Around 60 years old. Yes. 58, 60 years old.
I was asking about the Cootie Williams teacher. This man did teach Cootie. He was in Lipson. Lipson was really his teacher. I didn't know for sure if that was true.
His name was Charlie Lipson. That's right. He did teach Cootie.
And he's still living?

No, he's not. Oh, he's not living. He's not living. Now, he turned the band over to Lancaster. He's taken the band after I had given it up and turned it over to Lancaster. In other words, Lancaster's taken it up. Yes.
Yes.
Cootie Williams played with me quite a bit.
Are they professional musicians or do they have another job now? They don't play music.
They had other jobs.
Yes. Are they members of the union or are they...
Yes, they're all members of the union. They're all members of the union. I organized the American Federation of Musicians. In fact, I had it organized right here in Mobile.
Yes. I suppose some of them play in dance bands now, do they? Yes. Local dance bands?

Yes, I think so. Quite a few of them. But back in my days, we always had four or five orchestras in Mobile. Now, I think they have one. Yes. That's normal. I haven't heard of them myself. In fact, I've given up music now. It's been 25 years now.
You haven't played at all?
I haven't played at all. In fact, you don't own an instrument. Yes.

A friend of ours in New Orleans, Bill Matthews, a trombone player, has his own band. And he told us a few names to look up. One man, he didn't remember his last name. He said, Charlie, a trumpet player, had a pressing shop on Davis Avenue down near town. What kind of shop? He's not pressing, press closed. That's Charlie. That's Charlie. That's Charlie. Yes, he's dead. And I couldn't look at him. Yes, he made it. And another man he mentioned to see was Frank Jackson, a band.

Frank Jackson, he played with me. He played with you? He played with me. Is he still living? In my orchestra. Yes, but he's living in South Carolina somewhere. Oh, he's not here then. Yeah, Mobile. Yes. Very good. And I don't know of anyone else now that's around that could give me any information.
I was going to ask if you ever played on wagons when you, over in New Orleans, they advertised on wagons.
Yes, we have done that. You did do that? Yes. They advertised on big trucks, you know, one corner to another. They advertised the days to nine.
Mm-hmm. How many players did, how many musicians did you get on the wagons?

Well, we've mostly done that now in orchestra way. We had around 78 members. Yes, standard dance orchestra. Of course, I do remember back, we set some of that wagons with you in one of the salsa band. We'd have the whole band on the truck.
What sort of pieces did you play in the early days for dance music? Did you play polkas and things like that? Polkas. You did?
Charleston, waltzes. Then we played the lances.
Oh, yes. Is that the same as the quadrille about?
That's the same as the quadrille. Yes. We played all those dates with Viking Go's dance.
I was going to ask about the earliest dance music you heard. Did they use the banjo or guitar? In the band you have brass?
Yes. No, we did not. Just 14 brass pieces.
Yes, but I mean, they did use another small dance band.
Oh, small band, yes, my band. We had, I have a guitar player right now. He came to the Bears Mugger on the fuel right now from Philly Duffin.
Which did they use first, the banjo or the guitar, any oldest? They used the banjo first.
Banjo was first. Yeah. Do you remember when you first heard ragtime music?
When I first heard it? Yes.
When did you first hear ragtime music?
Well, ragtime music, I'm saying we were right there in our mobile year. We played some ragtime music, but New Orleans was famous for that, you know.
You probably learned it from people from New Orleans. That's right. That's right. About 1900 probably?
Well, that was about 19... ...eight. Nineteen eight. Nineteen nine, something like that. Yes.
The old bass players, when they played the string bass, did they use a bow or did they pick?

Very southern, they used to pick. They used to pick here most of them. That's right. Very southern they used the bow. I think the best violin player we had come through here was Sam Morgan's brother. I guess you remember those mugs. Yes, I know. Well, he used to use the bow. I think he was the only one that played by music, I think. And he took that up away from me.
Yes. Did you used to use mutes?
Mutes, yes, sure.
You did. Yes, yes.
Flat on.
One other question is, did they ever use a violin in the dance bands?
Yes, we have.
In the orchestra? Yes, that's right. Sure. He played violin. Someone else I can't remember right now, back in those days. I suppose the violin player
was the leader. Was he the leader of the orchestra? Well, he was leader of his own.

That's one I have reference to. When I left him, I organized my own orchestra and I was leader of that band. Quite a long time. And you had a violin in that band too? He played with me at times. Actually played violin in his own band. I played with him. I was trumpet playing in his band.
There were a couple of other famous New Orleans carnet players. One was Buddy Bold.

Did you ever hear him? I don't remember him, but I do remember Emmanuel Teres. Oh, yes. Do you remember him? Yes, I met him. I knew him. He died too. I didn't hear him play. Yeah, right. He always compared me with Perry. He used to come over here. Yeah, he did. I used to show off a little bit, you know, when he'd be in town, you know, I'd make some passengers there. And he'd say, you know, those fellas there, they can't do that, you know, like you like it.
Did you ever hear Joe Oliver? They called him King Oliver later?

Joe Oliver? Yes, I remember him in the early days. I think he used to play Yanmobili. He used to come over here and play for the next school. That's been quite a while now. Oh, yes, a long time. Yeah, I'm going way back. I remember quite a few out of the audience, but I just can't recall them now because I'm not prepared.
